title: The Shaved Head: Jerusalem Divided by Thirds
summary: God tells Ezekiel to shave his head and beard with a sword, weigh the hair, and divide it into thirds: one burned, one struck with the sword, one scattered to the wind, with a few strands tucked into his garment. God then explains the sign. Jerusalem, set at the center of the nations, has rebelled worse than they have, and she will be struck by plague, famine, sword, and scattering until she becomes a warning to the world.
story: Chapter 5 finishes the set of acted-out signs that began in chapter 4, where Ezekiel built a model of besieged Jerusalem, lay on his side for months, and ate rationed siege bread. Those signs showed the siege. This one shows its outcome: what happens to the people when the walls fail. It is the first time in the book that God explains a sign at length, and the explanation (verses 5 to 17) is one of the most severe speeches in the prophets. It sets the tone for the first half of Ezekiel, which is an argument, repeated in many forms, that Jerusalem will fall and that her fall is just. The few strands of hair in the prophet's garment are the book's first faint hint that God will preserve a remnant, a thread that grows much stronger in chapters 11, 36, and 37.
historical:
Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC, when the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II captured Jerusalem and deported King Jehoiachin along with many of the city's leading families. He lived among the exiles by the Kebar canal in southern Mesopotamia, and his call came in 593 BC (1:2). Back in Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar had installed Zedekiah as a vassal king. Many of the exiles expected to go home soon and assumed the city and its temple could not fall. Ezekiel's signs were aimed squarely at that confidence.

The siege he pictured came a few years later. Zedekiah rebelled, the Babylonian army surrounded Jerusalem from about 588 BC, and the city fell in 587 or 586 BC. The three fates in verse 12 (plague and famine inside, sword outside, scattering to the winds) describe how ancient sieges actually ended: disease and hunger inside the walls, slaughter of those who fled or fought, and deportation of the survivors. The Book of Lamentations and 2 Kings 25 record the same pattern after the fall.
cultural:
Shaving was loaded with meaning. In the ancient Near East, shaving the head and beard was a sign of mourning or of public disgrace, and the Law forbade priests to shave their heads or the edges of their beards (Leviticus 21:5). For Ezekiel, a priest, to shave himself with a sword was to act out humiliation, grief, and the collapse of holiness all at once. The sword doing the barber's work tells the watching exiles who the real barber will be: the invading army. Weighing the hair on scales suggests that the judgment is measured, not random.

The most terrible line, that parents and children will eat one another (verse 10), reflects what happened in real ancient sieges. The covenant curses in Leviticus 26:29 and Deuteronomy 28:53-57 had warned of it, 2 Kings 6:28-29 records it during an earlier siege of Samaria, and Lamentations 4:10 grieves that it happened in Jerusalem. Ezekiel is not inventing horrors; he is naming what the covenant had long said would follow if Israel abandoned its God. Verse 5 also draws on a common ancient idea that a people's holy city stood at the center of the world. God grants that Jerusalem was set “in the center of the nations,” and turns the privilege into the ground of her accountability.
literary: The chapter has two parts: a sign-act (verses 1 to 4) and its interpretation (verses 5 to 17). The interpretation is built from a chain of formulas that give it a hammering rhythm: “This is what the Lord GOD says,” then “Therefore,” then “Therefore” again, and finally the closing signature, “I, the LORD, have spoken,” in verses 15 and 17, with a fuller form of it in verse 13. The logic runs from privilege (verse 5), to rebellion (verses 6 and 7), to judgment (verses 8 to 17). The threefold division of the hair in verse 2 returns in verse 12 as the threefold fate of the people, which ties the sign tightly to its meaning. The list of plague, famine, sword, and wild beasts in verses 16 and 17 echoes the covenant curses of Leviticus 26, a list Ezekiel will use again in chapter 14.

outline.t: The sign: the prophet's hair shaved, weighed, and divided
Jerusalem at the center of the nations, and worse than them
The sanctuary defiled and the people divided by thirds
Wrath spent, and Jerusalem a warning to the nations

doctrines.note: Judgment here is measured and deserved. God judges Jerusalem by the standard of his own statutes, which she had received and rejected, and even by the ordinances of the nations, which she failed to meet (verse 7). Greater privilege brings greater accountability.

The heart of the charge is that Jerusalem “defiled My sanctuary” (verse 11). God's presence among his people is a gift that cannot be treated as a possession; a holy God will not stay where he is dishonored, a theme that becomes visible in chapters 8 to 11.

The disasters listed are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 coming due. Ezekiel presents the fall of Jerusalem not as a failure of God's promises but as God keeping his word, the warnings as well as the blessings.

words.note: Qin'ah, jealousy or zeal. In verse 13 God says he has spoken “in My zeal.” The word describes the passionate, exclusive commitment of a husband to his wife or of God to his people. It is not petty envy but the refusal to share what rightly belongs to him, which is why it so often appears alongside idolatry.

She'erit, remnant, what is left over. In verse 10 even the remnant will be scattered, which shows how thorough the judgment will be. Yet the strands of hair kept in the prophet's garment (verse 3) point toward the remnant theme that later prophets and Ezekiel himself develop: God preserves a people through judgment.

Miqdash, sanctuary, literally a holy place. The word comes from the root for holiness. Ezekiel, a priest, measures everything by what has happened to God's sanctuary, and the book will end, in chapters 40 to 48, with a vision of a new and purified one.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is thematic, not predictive. It shows the weight of covenant curse falling on a people who had broken the covenant, and it shows God preserving a small remnant through it. The New Testament speaks of Jesus as the one who bore the curse of the law on behalf of others (Galatians 3:13), so that the judgment pictured here in such dark detail is not the last word for those who trust him. Jesus also wept over Jerusalem and foretold another siege and fall (Luke 19:41-44; 21:20-24), speaking in the prophetic tradition that Ezekiel stands in, with the same grief over a city that did not recognize the time of God's coming.

hard.q: How can God say he will not pity or spare, and that his wrath will be spent, without seeming cruel?
hard.a: The difficulty is real, and the language is deliberately severe. Several things help to read it honestly. First, this is covenant speech: Israel had bound itself to God with blessings and curses spelled out in advance, and for generations the prophets had warned of these outcomes. Second, the wrath is not a loss of temper but a judicial response to specific wrongs named in the text, chiefly idolatry and the defiling of the temple, and later chapters add violence and injustice. Third, the phrase about wrath being spent (verse 13) implies that judgment has a limit and an end, and the book goes on to promise restoration (chapters 11, 36, 37). Some readers still find the images of cannibalism and slaughter too dark to reconcile with a loving God. The book does not soften them. Its answer is that sin against a holy God is terribly serious, and that God's final purpose is not destruction but a people who know him.

questions: Jerusalem's privilege (being set at the center of the nations) became the ground of her accountability. What privileges in your own life carry that kind of responsibility?
Why do you think God chose such a physical, shocking sign rather than words alone to reach the exiles?
The few strands of hair saved in the prophet's garment are easy to miss. Where have you seen small signs of mercy inside a season of judgment or loss?
